cases.learnTitle: Intracranial aneurysm on time-of-flight MR angiography (expert outline)
cases.clinicalContext: Adult referred for MR angiography of the head.
cases.contextSource: Dataset description (time-of-flight MR angiography at a university hospital); no clinical history is distributed.
cases.referenceSummary: The aneurysm was outlined voxel by voxel on the axial images by a radiologist with two years of neuroimaging experience and double-checked by a senior neuroradiologist (over 15 years). Ruptured, treated and fully thrombosed aneurysms were not part of the cohort. The arteries are not outlined by the dataset, and it does not record which artery the aneurysm arises from.
cases.learnNotes: A saccular (berry) aneurysm is a rounded outpouching of an artery wall, usually at a branching point of the Circle of Willis: the anterior communicating artery, the internal carotid artery at the origin of the posterior communicating artery, the middle cerebral artery bifurcation and the tip of the basilar artery. On time-of-flight MR angiography flowing blood is bright, so an aneurysm is a bright bulge attached to an artery. Scroll the thin source images first, then use a thick-slab MIP or the 3D view and check each branching point on both sides: a small aneurysm hides behind overlapping arteries on a single projection. Do not call a vessel loop or the funnel-shaped origin of a posterior communicating artery (an infundibulum, under 3 mm, with the artery leaving its apex) an aneurysm. Size and site decide the risk of rupture, and a ruptured aneurysm is the usual cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage (Learning Radiology, Ch. 26).

cases.learnTitle: Complete Circle of Willis on MR angiography (expert labels)
cases.clinicalContext: Adult; MR angiography of the head.
cases.contextSource: Dataset description (people without an aneurysm); no clinical history is distributed.
cases.referenceSummary: Each artery of the Circle of Willis is labelled by the TopCoW challenge annotators (research staff trained by clinical experts, uncertain cases decided with neuroradiologists), who also recorded which communicating segments are seen. The labels cover the circle and the first part of each artery; veins and branches beyond are not labelled.
cases.learnNotes: The Circle of Willis joins the two internal carotid arteries (front) and the basilar artery (back). Each internal carotid artery ends by dividing into the anterior cerebral artery (its first part, A1, runs medially to the anterior communicating artery; A2 runs up between the hemispheres) and the middle cerebral artery (M1 runs laterally to its division into M2 branches in the Sylvian fissure). The basilar artery ends by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries (P1 up to the posterior communicating artery, P2 beyond it, around the midbrain). The posterior communicating arteries link each internal carotid artery to its posterior cerebral artery. A complete circle is found in only a minority of people: a communicating artery or an A1/P1 segment is often too small to see. On a time-of-flight MRA a segment that is not seen may be absent or simply too small (slow flow), so call it 'not seen' rather than 'absent'.

tasks.explanation: The Circle of Willis joins the two internal carotid arteries (front) and the basilar artery (back). Each internal carotid artery ends by dividing into the anterior cerebral artery (its first part, A1, runs medially to the anterior communicating artery; A2 runs up between the hemispheres) and the middle cerebral artery (M1 runs laterally to its division into M2 branches in the Sylvian fissure). The basilar artery ends by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries (P1 up to the posterior communicating artery, P2 beyond it, around the midbrain). The posterior communicating arteries link each internal carotid artery to its posterior cerebral artery. A complete circle is found in only a minority of people: a communicating artery or an A1/P1 segment is often too small to see. On a time-of-flight MRA a segment that is not seen may be absent or simply too small (slow flow), so call it 'not seen' rather than 'absent'.
